svg.title: Four-Week Judgment Lifespan Audit
svg.desc: diagram id: diag-08-judgment-lifespan-roadmap; chapter number: 12; chart type: timeline_roadmap; title: Four-Week Judgment Lifespan Audit; subtitle: Logging expiry, renewing, checking revival windows, and sizing defense risk; caption: Judgments outlive the debts behind them only when renewal and revival deadlines are tracked; collectors who miss the window face debtors who check it.; assumptions note: The four-week sequence is an organizing frame, not a practitioner-reported timeline; lifespans, windows, and fees are as stated by the cited speakers and vary by state.; note: Sources - The Business Guy (nbtlIEi4we0), Law Office of Richard Kistnen (bkM9l8fajkc), The Credit Repair Shop (--FOsBTlu2E, 4Mctc4AuqWA), Consumer Warrior with John Skiba (fWHpyqQu_5M).; weeks: week: Week 1; title: Lifespan Audit; deliverable: Judgment date and state lifespan logged for every file, such as California 10 plus 10 and Oklahoma 5-year renewals indefinitely; gate: No file is worked until its expiry and renewal dates are calendared; week: Week 2; title: Renewal Filing; deliverable: Renewals filed where due, a simple filing for another 10 years per Kistnen; gate: Renewal goes through when the debtor does not appear to challenge it; week: Week 3; title: Revival Window Check; deliverable: State revival window checked against the original judgment date on every dormant purchased judgment; gate: Drop any revival past the window; one Ohio collector filed two years past a 10-year window; week: Week 4; title: Lawsuit and Arbitration Posture; deliverable: New suits sized against AAA fees of about $200 for the consumer versus $2,500 to $5,000 upfront for the creditor; gate: About 95 percent of sued consumers default, but a $3,500 claim compelled into AAA arbitration usually ends in dismissal or a mutual walk-away
